Chelsea hit the frame of the goal once more. Jackson gets the better of Vladimirov down Chelsea’s left and moves into the AC Milan penalty area. Jackson opens up his body as if he is going to curl his shot into the far corner but instead shoots towards the near corner, with his effort coming off the post.

Ricci goes for an audacious strike with the outside of his right foot from outside the box but his effort misses the target.

Palmer was deep in conversation with his boss Alonso during that water break.

Chelsea made a substitution during that break as Anselmino comes on for Hato. Thus far, Chelsea have made three changes in this game and Alonso did confirm before the game that some players should be able to go the full 90 this far into pre-season.

Chelsea hit the post. Quenda receives the ball on the right side of the penalty area and quickly moves the ball onto his right foot. The 19-year-old then smashes a shot towards goal and the ball flies into the outside of the post. Quenda struck that with some venom.

Palmer has a chance to get Chelsea’s fourth from the left side of the box but AC Milan keeper Torriani makes the save down to his left.

AC Milan have offered very little going forward since the break and Sanchez has not been troubled in the Chelsea goal.

AC Milan have a good chance to get a goal back. Musah finds space on the right side of the box and cuts it back towards the penalty spot. He picks out Nkunku but the former Chelsea man wastes the opportunity.

Palestra is found with a cross from the right to the far post. Palestra takes a touch but his shot goes into the side netting.

Ruben Amorim is demanding a free-kick just outside the Chelsea box but the referee does not agree. Replays show that AC Milan probably should have been given the free-kick as it was a foul by Fofana on Ramos. Both players went down but are back to their feet.

Xabi Alonso is going to make his first two changes of the game as Jackson and Quenda replace Welbeck and Neto.

Chelsea have their third and their new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee will be delighted with that one. Lavia plays a flat delivery from a corner out on the left to Caicedo on the edge of the box. Caicedo hits it first time on the volley with the outside of his right foot and picks out the bottom right corner with perfection.

Chelsea go 2-0 up not even a minute into the second half. Neto, on the right side of the box, cuts onto his preferred left foot and crosses to the far post. Pedro gets on the end of it and, despite the Milan keeper getting a touch on the shot, the ball ends up in the far corner.

AC Milan have made a raft of changes at the break, which includes their new record signing Ramos, who has joined from PSG this summer. Former Chelsea man Nkunku is also on. Milan were back out from the dressing rooms a fair bit earlier than Chelsea were. It is rather farcical how long Chelsea took to re-emerge for the second half and they just saunter out as if nothing is up. Why on earth did the officials just allow Chelsea to take over 20 minutes for half-time?

Nearly 25 minutes after the first half concluded, we are finally back under way in Jakarta.

Possession: Chelsea 58%-42% AC MilanShots: 6-4Shots on target: 3-0Corners: 4-2

The first half in Jakarta is brought an end and Chelsea take a 1-0 lead into the break courtesy of Pedro’s goal on the stroke of half-time.

90 seconds into added time at the end of this first half, we have the first goal in Jakarta. Caicedo’s delivery from the right picks out Pedro, who has a free header inside the six-yard box and makes no mistake, picking out the corner. Pedro really should not have been afforded so much space in the six-yard box.

Palestra makes a run in behind the AC Milan defence and is found but De Winter gets back to put it behind for a corner...

Due to the water break, there will be three additional minutes at the end of this first half.

The first booking of the game goes the way of AC Milan as Pavlovic clears out Palestra. A deserved booking.

Neto and Pedro exchange a good one-two down Chelsea’s right to put the former racing down the right wing. Neto then tries to find Welbeck in the centre of the box but it is just behind him.

Then, moments later, Pedro spurns a great chance for Chelsea. Palestra’s cross from the left is just out of Palmer’s reach but falls straight to Pedro, who blazes over from 12 yards out. He was leaning back and should really be hitting the target.

The space opens up for Palmer to take on a shot from range but his effort is blocked by De Winter. Palmer has not managed to have that much of an effect on this game thus far.

Pavlovic drives forward from his defensive position through the Chelsea half. He gets all the way to the Chelsea box before shooting but he looked to lack conviction, firing off target.

We will pause for a drinks break, which unfortunately we became accustomed to during the World Cup. Palmer takes the chance to take a seat on the bench whilst taking on some fluids.

Neto takes a first-time shot from outside the box and looks to curl it into the far corner, forcing Torriani into a decent save diving down to his right.

That is good one-vs-one defending from Achemapong. Estupinan plays the ball into the path of Leao, who drives through the Chelsea half down AC Milan’s left. As Leao approaches the Chelsea box, Leao attempts to push it past Acheampong but the young Chelsea defender times his sliding challenge to perfection and puts it behind for a corner. Sanchez punches it out to the edge of the box, where Comotto takes it on his chest before volleying towards goal. The ball goes behind for another corner, which Chelsea just about scramble away.

Chelsea hit the post. Palestra drives forward for Chelsea down their left before the ball falls to Welbeck on the left side of the box. Welbeck’s effort hits the outside of the post. AC Milan keeper Torriani appeared though to always have it covered.

Chelsea gift the ball away inside their own half and Leao drives forward. The Portuguese forward moves into the Chelsea penalty area before getting his shot away but his effort is blocked.

A big, big chance for Chelsea to take the lead. A long ball is played forward in behind the AC Milan defence and Pedro gets the better of De Winter inside the Milan penalty area. It is then a one-on-one chance with Torriani but Pedro hits it straight at the Milan goalkeeper. Torriani should have come to claim that long ball and then Pedro should probably have buried that opportunity.

Chelsea win their third corner of the game as Palmer’s cross from the right takes a couple of deflections off AC Milan defender. Captain Caicedo has trotted over to take it out on the left. He sends it into a good area but a foul on the AC Milan keeper Torriani is given against Pedro.

Neto clips a free-kick into the AC Milan penalty area, which is chested down by Pedro. The Brazilian holds the ball up well inside the box before winning a corner. Chelsea play it short and Palmer crosses to the back post, where Palestra wins Chelsea another corner, this time out on the left.

Caicedo’s inswinging delivery is headed away at the front post.

Palestra, who has joined Chelsea this summer from Atalanta, is proving his versatility today; he has mostly operated for Chelsea at right-back so far this pre-season but he is starting at left-back in this game.

Camarda is played in behind the Chelsea defence and tries to get the better of Fofana inside the Chelsea penalty area but the ball just runs out of play across the byline before Camarda can square the ball.

We are under way in Jakarta, Indonesia, in Chelsea’s penultimate game over in the Far East. Before the game started, a huge AC Milan tifo was unveiled at one end of the ground.

It is 7pm in Jakarta yet the temperature is still up at 29 degrees with the humidity at nearly 70%. These conditions will be a proper test for both sides.

The teams emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off in Indonesia.

The trophies won by Franco Baresi, who has died at the age of 66, are their own monument to the AC Milan and Italy defender’s greatness. Six times a Serie A champion, five as captain, three European Cup-winning campaigns, 10 other winners’ medals and the distinction of being a member of Italy squads that finished in first, second and third places at World Cup tournaments demonstrate that his career, in a significantly more meritocratic era, stand alongside the giants even if the bias towards attacking virtuosos denied him the Ballon d’Or his talent deserved.

Yet they do not tell us why the grief, so tangible in Milan and beyond today, transcends tribal rivalry. It would be unfair to say that he transformed the art of Italian defending. Gaetano Scirea, the elegant Juventus sweeper who kept the 21-year-old Baresi confined to the bench when Italy won their third World Cup in 1982, had a surplus of natural ability, composure and intelligence. He did not need the raw-elbowed brutality of Claudio Gentile, heir to generations of Italian defenders influenced by the post-war influx of players brought up in the traditions of Argentina and Uruguay.

INS:Marco Palestra ⇠ Atalanta, £42mGeovany Quenda ⇠ Sporting, £42mMorgan Rogers ⇠ Aston Villa, £117mMaxence Lacroix ⇠ Crystal Palace, £51mDanny Welbeck ⇠ Brighton, UndisclosedJordan Henderson ⇠ Brentford, FreeValentin Barco ⇠ Strasbourg, Undisclosed

OUTS:Andrey Santos ⇢ Manchester United, £50mMarc Cucurella ⇢ Real Madrid, £50mTyrique George ⇢ Everton, £24mAlejandro Garnacho ⇢ Aston Villa, Loan

Chelsea are on the verge of making yet another signing with Rayo Vallecano left-back Pep Chavarria close to securing a move to Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea: Sanchez; Palestra, Acheampong, Fofana, Hato; Palmer, Caicedo, Lavia, Neto; Welbeck, Joao Pedro.Substitutes: Sharman-Lowe, Penders, Sarr, Anselmino, Tosin, Subuloye, Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Watson, Walsh, Satpayev, Quenda, Gittens, Estevao, Mudryk, Jackson, Delap.

AC Milan: Torriani; Terracciano, De Winter, Pavlovic; Chukwueze, Modric, Comotto, Estupinan; Loftus-Cheek, Leao; Camarda.Substitutes: Ricci, G. Ramos, Diawara, Nkunku, Fofana, Tomori, Athekame, Odogu, Jashari, Bartesaghi, Vladimirov, Pittarella, Gabbia, Saelemakers, Cisse, Musah.

The English forward joined Chelsea from Borussia Dortmund last summer for just under £50m. He struggled to make an impact last season in his first year at Chelsea, failing to register a goal in the Premier League or Champions League but did spend most of the second half of last season on the sidelines due to an injury. Gittens, who is on the bench for Chelsea today, has been speaking this week to CFC+:

“I am feeling, I would say, more confident now, in my body as well. The injury that happened [impacted my first season], but I am feeling better every day. I am trying to improve every day to be the best version of myself. It has been good to be back with the boys. I am really enjoying it right now and it has been really good to be part of this team.”

Have a great day, Jamie. 🥳 pic.twitter.com/QeX83XrXAM

In Chelsea’s defeat to Juventus in midweek, Ukrainian forward Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 after a long doping ban was resolved. You can read all about that game right here. Mudryk is on the bench for Chelsea today.

Our line-up to face AC Milan! pic.twitter.com/MK2hd0c708

The atmosphere is building. 🇮🇩📈 pic.twitter.com/fhXfDVAf6s

Chelsea’s pre-season continues out in the Far East as they take on AC Milan in the Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta, Indonesia. Both clubs now have new managers, with Xabi Alonso taking over at Chelsea and former Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim now at the helm at AC Milan. These sides met in pre-season last year, with Chelsea winning 4-1 at Stamford Bridge. At that time, now-Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca was in charge whilst Max Allegri, who is now at Napoli, was leading AC Milan. The last time they met competitively was during the 2022/23 Champions League season, with Chelsea winning both games.

Chelsea lost 1-0 to AC Milan’s Serie A rivals Juventus on Wednesday in Hong Kong, in which Danny Welbeck made his first Chelsea appearance after joining from Brighton in the last week.

“We want to have a great team spirit and that is built on a daily basis with a great culture in the building,” Alonso said in his pre-match press conference. “That helps in the moment you have to compete. You feel better having that togetherness, trust, and the bonds between the players are so important to ultimately building a winning mentality, and a team that can compete anywhere. So the football side is so important, but the mental side is as important. And the strength of the team is the most important. We have been able to train and prepare [during pre-season] and I am very happy with the attitude and personality, we know that it is a very important part of this tour.”

It has been another busy week on the transfer front for Chelsea; not only has Welbeck arrived over the last week but so too have Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco. Alonso’s men have two more games after this against Johor Darul Ta’zim and Real Sociedad before getting their Premier League campaign under way with a derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage.

AC Milan finished fifth in Serie A last season to earn a spot in the Europa League last season. Their big-money acquisition this summer as been Portuguese striker Goncalo Ramos from PSG. They have played two pre-season friendlies so far, which have both ended in draws; 2-2 against Celtic and then 1-1 against city rivals Inter. They kick off their Serie A campaign at Torino on August 23.

#2132. Arsenal injury latest: Konsa concern, Saliba return and Saka update

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal will hope Ezri Konsa recovers in time for Saturday’s 3pm Premier League clash with Hull City after he came off during their Champions League win over Slavia Prague.The return of William Saliba to the matchday squad is a great boost for Mikel Arteta ahead of the game, but Bukayo Saka remains out as he continues to recover from his quad injury.

Here is all the latest Arsenal injury news and when the three players are expected to return.

Konsa started Arsenal’s 2-1 victory over Slavia Prague on Wednesday but came off in the second half after experiencing discomfort.

He appeared to limp during the first half, so Arsenal will monitor his fitness closely ahead of Saturday’s match.

Arteta said the change was not a tactical one, as Konsa had been playing a lot of games recently and had some problems during the match.

The Arsenal boss is likely to give an update ahead of Saturday’s game depending on how he recovers in the coming days.

Konsa’s absence will leave Arsenal without as many reliable centre backs. However, Gabriel will play a key role in the backline, and Arteta has other options in Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie.

Potential return date: November 7 vs Hull City (3pm kick-off).

A positive from the Gunners’ trip to Prague was the inclusion of Saliba in the squad.

The defender has not played this season after picking up a long-term back injury. The issue got worse during his time with France at the World Cup finals, but he managed to avoid surgery.

Saliba has steadily built up his workload and played for 45 minutes in a behind-closed-moors game. He returned to full training on Tuesday and travelled with the squad to take on Slavia Prague.

Although he did not come off the bench, his inclusion shows he is getting close to being back in contention.

Arteta said that Saliba was feeling confident, but it will depend on the needs of the squad.

It gives Arsenal an extra experienced centre-back, and if Konsa is not available against Hull, then he could make an appearance on the pitch.

Potential return date: November 7 vs Hull City (3pm kick-off).

Saka is currently the main attacking concern for Arsenal after he has been sidelined with a quad injury for the last four games.

The winger suffered the injury approximately 10 minutes into the Arsenal Champions League clash against Bayern Munich last month.

The original fears were that Saka would be out for up to eight weeks. Arsenal have not given any confirmation on how long it will take him to make a full recovery.

He will need to undergo another scan to get a better idea of the amount of swelling and fluid in the area. The medical staff will also want to see if the tendon is involved.

This means it is unlikely he plays against Hull. Arsenal are not expected to bring him back too quickly ahead of the international break.

Arteta will miss one of his most influential attackers. Hopefully the next scan will give a clearer indication of how long he is likely to be out for.

Expected return date: Unknown. Saka is not expected to face Hull City on November 7.

Arsenal host Hull City at the Emirates Stadium on Saturday, November 7th.

The game comes ahead of a tough sequence of games which sees Manchester City, Real Madrid and Tottenham on the horizon. Arteta will want as many defensive and attacking threats on hand.

#2131. Amorim analyses how Milan were able to overpower Inter: “High pressure and low blocking”

AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim refused to be drawn into discussions about the Scudetto, even if he does see improvements from his side.

Milan were in dreamland after 45 minutes of their derby clash against Inter, going in 3-1 up at the break thanks to goals from Christian Pulisic, Adrien Rabiot and Diego Moreira. As it would turn out, that would be enough to win the bragging rights.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It marked a fourth straight win for Milan in the derby and it reduces the gap to the city rivals back down to four points. While there is still work to be done for the Rossoneri, it feels like a big step forward mentally for the squad.

Amorim spoke to Sky after the full-time whistle to reflect on what was a memorable night for him as a head coach and for the team, with his words relayed by MilanNews.

Is this the most important victory of the start of the season?

“It’s important. The atmosphere is fantastic, and you can tell after a match like that, especially on a Wednesday like this. It’s clear, even more so after the defeat against Bologna, we wanted to celebrate even more.

“I’m really proud of what my players did, and with so little rest between matches, and especially once again after Bologna, they really fought for the entire match. I’m really proud.”

A nearly perfect team: do you have anything to complain about? You seemed calmer today…

“I try to read and interpret what the team tells me: from the first minute I had the feeling that we were ready to be competitive. The team has always been focused and calm, and so I always had this confidence.”

Is AC Milan a different Milan with Modric, Rabiot, and Pulisic?

“It’s not just those three players, I think it’s the whole atmosphere, the team’s focus. I like the way everyone plays and expresses themselves. For example, I’d like to talk a little about Pavlović and De Vrij.

“They performed well in every game, especially against such a strong team, even in the penalty area. And then, obviously, players like Rabiot, Pulisic, Moreira… they all did very well. All together, I have to say, we were a better team.”

Why Gila on the right and De Winter in the centre?

“Looking at Inter’s stats, we didn’t know if Dimarco would play. They play and cross a lot from the wings and come to create a lot of density in the box, so I think Pavlović and De Winter are the best for crossing.

“That’s the idea: to match our defenders with their attackers, so everyone can play in slightly different defensive roles.”

How did you manage not to concede anything to Inter in the second half?

“I think the lines were closer together; you could see that throughout the match in terms of high pressure and low blocking. The lines were always close together, so the distances were shorter, which obviously also allowed us to run less and stay fresher throughout the game.

“We were very aggressive on the outside, intercepting many crosses before they were launched, which is very difficult against a team like Inter. We defended well by pressing high up, but we also defended well on the sides. We were more aggressive than we usually are.”

“What Cardinale was saying is that the objective is the Scudetto, but it’s important to win these games to make the fans understand that things won’t change in a month, two months, or a year.

“We have to go through this process: you can’t just hire a new coach, replace all the players, and have a new squad for each new coach; that takes time. Then we’ll need magical nights and evenings, and obviously we’ll need to get through difficulties like Wednesday’s and the joy of tonight.

“I want to say that the situation won’t change overnight; it’s not possible. Is the Scudetto possible? I don’t know when, but we still have to be very honest with the fans, and I know that people aren’t stupid; they understand and know the growth this team and this club are in.”

#2130. Scott Parker’s Promotion Blueprint Offers West Ham A Way Forward

With Scott Parker set to become West Ham United’s new head coach, I’ve been looking back at his three Championship promotion campaigns to get a better idea of what supporters can expect. Rather than simply guessing how he’ll set up the Hammers, I wanted to examine the formations and players he actually used at Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham.

And having looked through the evidence, I’m increasingly convinced that Parker will favour a 4-2-3-1 at West Ham. It was his preferred system during Burnley’s remarkable 2024/25 promotion campaign, and he also used it at both Bournemouth and Fulham, although he was prepared to switch formations when necessary.

As discussed earlier today, his record of securing promotion with three different clubs was always likely to appeal to West Ham’s decision-makers. But it’s the way he achieved those promotions that interests me, particularly given the problems we’ve witnessed under Nuno Espírito Santo.

Parker’s record is impressive enough without dressing it up. He took Fulham up through the play-offs in 2020, secured automatic promotion with Bournemouth in 2022 and then guided Burnley back to the Premier League with 100 points in 2025.

What I found particularly interesting was that all three sides used a 4-2-3-1 in their final promotion-season matches. That doesn’t mean Parker played the formation every week, but it does provide a useful starting point when trying to establish his tactical preferences.

Those figures show the goals conceded across each 46-match league campaign, rather than just the final matches. And the progression is interesting, with Parker’s most recent promotion-winning team producing by far his strongest defensive record.

However, there’s an important distinction between his Bournemouth and Burnley sides. According to the Premier League’s tactical analysis, Bournemouth actually used 4-3-3 on 27 occasions during their promotion campaign, compared with 13 starts in 4-2-3-1. Parker increasingly favoured the latter towards the end of the season.

Burnley, on the other hand, were much more closely associated with 4-2-3-1. The Premier League’s examination of their promotion campaign identified it as Parker’s first-choice formation, with two midfielders providing defensive protection and the number ten contributing heavily to the press.

To give you lovely C&H readers a clearer picture, I’ve taken the starting elevens from Fulham’s 2020 play-off final victory against Brentford and Burnley’s final Championship fixture against Millwall in 2025.

Both were recorded as 4-2-3-1, although the responsibilities of individual players were not identical.

The obvious similarity is the presence of two central midfielders behind three more advanced players. That’s the aspect of the formation I find particularly appealing for West Ham.

I’ve already seen plenty of people complaining about Parker’s supposedly negative football, but I find that criticism slightly strange when you look at what he achieved at Burnley.

Sixteen goals conceded in 46 Championship games is incredible. Make no mistake about it. His team also recorded 30 clean sheets, a remarkable achievement which helped Burnley finish the season with 100 points.

Burnley scored 69 goals that season, compared with Leeds United’s 95. So there is a legitimate discussion to be had about whether Parker’s football can sometimes be too cautious, but I certainly wouldn’t dismiss the defensive record as a negative.

In fact, I would expect the first priority of any manager arriving at West Ham to be fixing the defence. It’s crap.

There’s a certain irony here, of course. West Ham had the most porous defence in the Premier League when Nuno Espírito Santo arrived last season, and we all remember how Graham Potter’s team seemingly couldn’t defend a corner. Improving that situation was supposed to be one of Nuno’s principal jobs.

Yet in the end, we were left with a pragmatic defensive manager who had seemingly forgotten how to park the bus.

As Nuno’s dismissal following the defeat against West Bromwich Albion demonstrated, the club eventually ran out of patience with performances that were neither defensively convincing nor particularly effective going forward.

I think Parker’s defensive organisation is precisely what West Ham should be looking for now. And if that improved structure can give our more creative players a little extra freedom, then so much the better.

Nuno was brought in to fix Potters awful defence

Looking at Parker’s previous teams, I believe 4-2-3-1 would be a sensible fit for the players he is inheriting at West Ham. The formation provides two central midfielders who can protect the defence, which should immediately help address the problems we’ve had with opponents dominating the middle of the pitch.

But the benefit isn’t purely defensive. Having that protection behind the attacking players should allow them to operate with considerably more freedom, rather than constantly worrying about what happens when possession is lost.

It also provides something I believe West Ham have desperately needed: a proper number ten.

And I don’t mean somebody like Mohamedou Kanté being shoehorned into a false-nine position he’s not equipped for. I mean a genuine playmaker with an eye for a pass, a stepover and a trick, somebody capable of unlocking a defence rather than simply occupying a position on the pitch.

That’s where Divine Mukasa comes into it for me, although I could also see Manor Solomon operating in that role.

I think either could benefit from having two midfielders behind them, particularly if Jarrod Bowen is given the freedom to get into more dangerous attacking positions.

Of course, there’s an important qualification here. Parker’s Burnley number ten was often expected to work extremely hard without the ball, pressing opponents and helping protect the midfield. So it would be wrong to assume he will automatically select a traditional playmaker simply because he uses 4-2-3-1.

Nevertheless, the formation offers that possibility, and I think it’s one West Ham’s attacking players would hopefully enjoy playing in.

There’s another reason I’m reluctant to accept the suggestion that Parker can only produce negative football.

His Bournemouth team were particularly effective at pressing opponents during their promotion season. The Premier League’s tactical analysis recorded them as the Championship’s most intense pressing side by passes per defensive action, with opponents averaging just 10.8 passes before Bournemouth intervened defensively.

That suggests a manager who is capable of setting up a team to win the ball back aggressively, rather than simply sitting deep and hoping to nick a goal.

Bournemouth also conceded only 39 league goals during that campaign, demonstrating that Parker was able to combine a relatively aggressive approach without sacrificing defensive organisation.

And that’s really what I’d like to see at West Ham.

I’m not expecting Parker to turn us into some sort of attacking footballing circus, nor do I think fans should judge him on whether every game produces three or four goals.

But I do expect a team that knows its jobs, defends properly, competes from the first whistle and provides enough attacking support for its better players to make a difference.

The evidence from his previous promotion campaigns suggests Parker is capable of delivering that sort of structure. Whether he can reproduce it at West Ham remains to be seen, but there are genuine reasons for optimism.

Three promotions with three different clubs, a remarkable defensive record at Burnley and a clear history of using systems that could suit West Ham’s attacking players.

For me, that’s a far more useful way of assessing Scott Parker than simply dismissing him as a negative manager before he’s even started.

#2129. Your 'loud and crazy' supporters won't stop us winning at Celtic Park

Former Arsenal star Leandro Trossard has warned Celtic that Besiktas are coming to Parkhead determined to take three points.

The Belgian international believes his side can handle the famous Celtic Park atmosphere as they look to continue their impressive Europa League campaign. Trossard joined the Turkish giants from Arsenal in the summer and has set his sights on going deep into the competition.

Celtic are still searching for their first points of the league phase following a defeat to Celta Vigo last time out, while Besiktas have enjoyed a strong start.

And Trossard insists the visitors will not be intimidated by the Parkhead crowd. He said: “We want to get three points from the Celtic match. It will be very tough. They have loud and crazy fans, but if we can translate what we want onto the pitch, then we will win. [SunSport]

“Our fans should continue their support. It would be great if they increased this amazing backing. People don’t pay any attention to it, but the support from the fans is incredibly effective in difficult times. We have won matches with their support.

Homegrown Besiktas insider offers Celtic intel ahead of European showdown

“They can be sure that if they continue to get behind us, we will win even the toughest matches.”

Besiktas sit fourth in the Turkish league but have made an impressive start in Europe, collecting seven points from their opening three matches against Marseille, Hoffenheim and Crystal Palace.

Trossard believes there is even more to come as they target a place among the Europa League’s top eight. He added: “I’m very excited and we want to reach the top in Europe. The decisive factor is the draw and the team’s performance during these next few games.

“Our current goal is to be in the top eight. After that, we just need to see how things progress. Every player wants to win trophies and to be champions. They want to be at the top at the end of the league.

“We want to reach the best possible position in Europe and there’s also the Turkish Cup. Besiktas aims for trophies in every competition. We have got this potential and we can do it.

"There were matches where we could have played better, but there’s a new coach, a new team, and an adaptation process - I know we can do better things.”

#2128. West Ham’s big guns come out with verdict over Scott Parker appointment

Whilst officially West Ham United head into the midweek fixture against Cardiff City without a head coach, the Irons will mix the talents of established coaching duo Gerard Prenderville and Steve Potts with the expertise of sporting director Mark Noble to provide the off-field leadership for tonight’s attempt to arrest their two-game losing run and put some points on the board.

It will be intriguing to see the immediate impact which the sacking of Nuno Epirito Santo has on the Hammers’ dressing room when the whistle blows tonight.

Hopefully that means the end of ‘outcast’ squad members and that players will get utilised within their established positions soon enough, so that the era of square pegs being pushed into round holes is finally ended.

Many will feel relieved that the days of the division of the Hammers’ squad are ended: Now perhaps the handbrake could come off for the careers of several ‘outcasts’.

Behind the scenes the appointment of Scott Parker does seem nailed on, whilst no official pronouncement has yet been made. All roads point to the former Hammer of the Year taking control of the West Ham squad, which is an appointment that has already been welcomed by former players – one a former assistant to David Moyes who is, of course, still pretty close to the club.

Kevin Nolan, former captain during West Ham’s last promotion winning campaign, pronounced judgement on TalkSPORT:

“I’m delighted with the talk that it’s Scotty going in, giving a young British manager an opportunity at a big club. He’s got a track record. It’s going to be a tough season”

Former Irons’ striker turned TV pundit Dean Ashton was similarly positive. Speaking on talksport, Ashton pointed out that West Ham supporters hadn’t had a manager who felt connected with them for many years, but all that would change if and when Parker is confirmed:

“They want to be inspired again. It is important to connect again with the supporters… He’s certainly got fire in his belly and will relish the opportunity to manage West Ham.”

Whilst some fans profess disappointment over the ‘low ambition’ shown by the football club in considering Scott Parker, I’d suggest they’ve picked exactly the right man to do the job.

Forget the long term. Climb the greasy pole out of this hugely challenging division at all costs and back in the Premier League first. Then worry about what kind of football you want to play.

Because failure carries unthinkable financial repercussions for this football club. Right now, I’d suspect on track records alone, there’s nobody better qualified than former West Ham captain Scott Parker to do the job required.

#2127. West Ham Exclusive: Nuno Meeting Brought Sacking Forward

Claret & Hugh can reveal this morning that West Ham United dismissed Nuno Espírito Santo earlier than originally planned following a meeting between the head coach and club executives on Monday morning.

West Ham had become increasingly concerned about results and performances, and Nuno’s position was already under considerable scrutiny. The club had sounded out various potential replacements, including Scott Parker, but the intention had been to assess the situation over the next two Championship fixtures against Cardiff City and Blackburn Rovers.

However, that timetable changed following Monday’s meeting, during which Nuno would ordinarily have been expected to review the previous match and discuss plans for the January transfer window. Instead, the decision was taken to dismiss him with immediate effect, bringing his time at West Ham to an abrupt end.

As Claret & Hugh reported before Nuno’s dismissal, there had been growing concern within the club’s hierarchy about the direction of the team. However, the expectation had been that the Portuguese coach would have the Cardiff and Blackburn matches to demonstrate that he could turn things around.

That changed on Monday lunchtime. Quite what happened during the meeting has not been disclosed, but it would be fair to say that the outcome was not what Nuno would have been hoping for. Perhaps, and this is purely speculation on my part, he failed to provide the answers or assurances West Ham’s executives were seeking.

Whatever the precise circumstances, the decision meant Nuno would not be taking training on Tuesday morning. Instead, the club moved quickly to accelerate its search for a replacement, with Scott Parker emerging as the leading candidate to take charge.

Parker was rushing into West Ham ahead of schedule

The former Hammers midfielder was subsequently lined up for a two-and-a-half-year contract, with West Ham determined to have their new manager in place as quickly as possible.

As we revealed yesterday, Parker’s proposed agreement includes clauses linked to securing promotion back to the Premier League, while Nuno’s departure is expected to cost the club just under £3million in compensation.

The speed of the change has created an unusual situation ahead of tonight’s Championship trip to Cardiff City. Mark Noble has been overseeing preparations alongside Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville, although Claret & Hugh understands Parker will attend the match and could have some influence on team selection.

The rest, as they say, is history. West Ham had been preparing to give Nuno another two games, but Monday’s meeting brought that process to an unexpectedly early conclusion.

And while we may never discover precisely what was said behind closed doors, tonight’s trip to Wales provides an immediate opportunity for the players to put a dreadful couple of weeks behind them and begin moving forward under a new regime.

#2126. Man Utd impress in draw against PSG but injury worries mount

Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.

Mount has had a torrid time with injuries since signing from Chelsea in a £55m-deal three years ago, starting only 25 Premier League games for United in that time.

The 27-year-old has been successfully deployed by Carrick in a central midfield role during pre-season, leading to speculation that United may not make another expected signing in that department.

But Mount played only 18 minutes of Saturday’s 1-1 draw against the European champions in Gothenburg before being replaced by Scotland international Tyler Fletcher.

“He [Mount] got kicked. We just wanted to be careful and look after him,” Carrick, the United head coach, told reporters in Sweden.

“We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful.”

Post-match video footage showed Mount walking freely on to the United bus without the aid of a protective boot or knee support.

Michael Carrick told VG Mason Mount was taken off as a precaution. Looked OK leaving stadium. pic.twitter.com/Uo0fBtgpAl

United went behind within two minutes at the Ullevi Stadium when Liverpool target Ibrahim Mbaye punished slack marking to put PSG ahead.

Bryan Mbeumo fired United level after 32 minutes following good work from Amad Diallo, the Cameroon forward’s third goal in two games after his match-winning double against Atletico Madrid.

United meet Leeds in a Dublin friendly on Wednesday before coming up against AC Milan and their former manager Ruben Amorim next Saturday.

United open their Premier League campaign at Hull on August 22.

“It was good game. PSG is good so we had to keep building fitness. I am happy to have other [players] back and we have to keep going.”

“It’s good for me. I enjoyed it. We need to build fitness, we have a big season ahead.”

“It’s a good game PSG are tough to beat and we got a draw and now think about the next game [against Leeds in Dublin].”

“We have two more games against Leeds a and Milan. We need to have big season and hope to win a trophy.”

Manchester United continue their Sweden sojourn with match against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg.

Clearly a clash against the back-to-back Champions League winners is a step up from their previous two pre-season friendlies (victories against Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid), but at the same time this is more a chance for players to get miles in the legs and see how new signings and possibly some young guns fit in.

One of those new signings is Youri Tielemans, and the Belgian international is in line to make his debut after his move from Aston Villa. Other team news is that Bruno Fernandes is back and ready to captain the team.

Michael Carrick has also been boosted by the returns of Matheus Cunha, Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui after their post-World Cup breaks.

Cunha, however, will not play a part in today’s match because of a “minor illness” according to the MUTV website. He is expected to link up with the squad in Ireland, where they face Leeds United at Croke Park, after the match.

This will be Man Utd’s first outing since the 2-1 win over Atletico, a performance and result that pleased Carrick.

“I enjoyed it, I thought there was a lot of good in things that we are looking to improve on,” the United manager said. “Building on what we did for the last seven months, I think there is a lot of good signs for us, it’s never going to be the exact stage we want to be at. But I thought there was really a lot of positives to take out of the game, individual, collectively as a team, senior players looking strong and fit, and the younger players doing really well.

“The spirit and the camaraderie is so important for the team, it’s great to see the boys getting on so naturally and enjoying each other’s company. Collectively we looked strong as a team, which is always the most important thing, and individual performances seeing the young players come on to have an impact.”

Stefano recorded his reaction to AC Milan’s crucial win against Inter straight after the full-time whistle, highlighting the individual brilliance that got them over the line.

The Derby della Madonnina is always a special game and one you want to win, but Milan were under a bit more pressure to do so this evening. An unbeaten run to maintain, a gap to decrease in the standings and a point to prove after a poor mid-week display.

#2124. Scott Parker Confirmed As West Ham Boss – And He’s Ready For Cardiff

West Ham United have officially confirmed the appointment of Scott Parker as our new head coach, with the former Hammers captain signing a two-and-a-half-year contract. The announcement also confirms that Parker will take charge of tonight’s Championship fixture against Cardiff City, rather than Mark Noble, who had been overseeing preparations following Nuno Espírito Santo’s dismissal.

In a statement published on the official West Ham website, the club confirmed that Parker will be supported by Steve Potts, Gerard Prenderville and Billy Lepine, while Noble will work closely with his former teammate. Further details of the permanent coaching structure will be announced in due course.

Parker returns to West Ham having achieved promotion from the Championship with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley. It’s an impressive record and, with the Hammers desperate to return to the Premier League at the first attempt, I think there are plenty of reasons to be excited about his appointment.

Speaking following his appointment, Parker made it clear just how much returning to West Ham means to him.

“It is a very proud moment for me to step into this role and return to a Club that means so much to me and my family.”

The new manager also spoke passionately about his determination to secure promotion, pointing to his previous Championship experience and the importance of bringing consistency to West Ham’s performances.

“I’ve been in this division three times and I’ve got out of this division three times.”

That experience is precisely what West Ham need at the moment, but it’s not the only reason I’m looking forward to seeing Parker in the dugout.

I’ve got to say, I’m pretty excited about Scott Parker coming in. He wouldn’t necessarily have been my first choice, but I think his passion and enthusiasm will represent a real change from the softly spoken Nuno Espírito Santo. West Ham are a club that need a demonstrative manager on the touchline, somebody who looks as though he’s kicking every ball alongside the players.

I want to see a manager who communicates, motivates and shows the same urgency that we expect from the team. Parker has always struck me as somebody who understands what West Ham means to its supporters, and I think that connection could be particularly important after a difficult few months.

As Nuno’s departure demonstrated, something needed to change at the London Stadium. Parker now has an immediate opportunity to lift the players, improve performances and get West Ham’s promotion campaign moving in the right direction.

There is also something reassuring about having Parker, Noble and Potts involved in the club’s footballing setup. They understand West Ham, they know what supporters expect, and there should be no shortage of passion in the dugout.

Of course, none of that guarantees results, but I’m pleased with the appointment. We’ve brought in somebody who knows the Championship, understands West Ham and genuinely wants to be here.

#2123. West Ham Had No Choice But to End the Nuno Era – Here’s Why

“Stale.” It’s a simple word, but one that perfectly sums up the final months of Nuno Espírito Santo’s reign at West Ham United.

The football had become predictable, uninspiring and, all too often, difficult to watch. What arrived with optimism and expectation slowly descended into frustration and stagnation, leaving us supporters increasingly detached from a side that looked incapable of building momentum.

A win rate of just 35.8%, made up of 19 victories, 19 defeats and 15 draws, is hardly the return expected from a manager reportedly earning a basic £4.5 million per year. Add in performance-related bonuses that could have taken that figure beyond £5.5 million and the value for money argument becomes even harder to defend.

Much has already been written about Nuno’s career, his close relationship with football super-agent Jorge Mendes and his previous managerial successes and failures. However, the issues at West Ham appeared to run far deeper than results alone.

Reports of dressing-room unrest became increasingly difficult to ignore. The reaction from several players on social media following the club’s announcement of Nuno’s departure painted a picture that suggested not everyone was disappointed to see the back of the Portuguese coach.

Whether fair or not, perceptions matter, and by the time the board made its decision, it appeared they had little room left to manoeuvre.

Frequent tactical changes, constant rotation and regular shifts in formation left players struggling to develop understanding and rhythm. Too often the team looked unsure of its identity. One week brought a back three, the next a back four. Players found themselves moved in and out of the side without any obvious continuity.

The consequence was a team that never truly settled.

That is not to absolve the players of responsibility. Several underperformed throughout the campaign, regardless of the system being deployed. Ultimately, however, modern football remains a results business and the head coach is invariably the man held accountable when things go wrong.

Rightly or wrongly, that responsibility now sits firmly in the past.

The former Bournemouth and Burnley manager arrives with a clear brief, reignite confidence, restore belief and turn one of the Championship’s most talented squads into a genuine automatic promotion contender.

The challenge is significant, but so is the opportunity.

Tonight’s fixture against Cardiff City comes too early for Parker to have much influence, with the interim coaching team of Potts, Robson, Noble and Prenderville overseeing proceedings. However, it offers the first step in what supporters hope will be a fresh start.

The Nuno Espírito Santo chapter closes with disappointment, underachievement and a lingering sense of what might have been. Whether the blame lies with the manager, the players, or both, the reality is simple: The project failed to deliver.

Now comes the hard part. West Ham’s season is still alive, but the margin for error has all but disappeared. If promotion is to be achieved, the talent within this squad must finally translate into performances on the pitch.

The Nuno era ended exactly as it had become, Stale.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2122. Lewis Ferguson insists Rangers move 'will happen' in big transfer declaration

Lewis Ferguson has revealed he expects to play for Rangers one day as the Scotland star opened up on his future.

The Bologna captain has established himself as one of the leading Scottish players abroad after moving to Italy in 2022, with his performances regularly prompting speculation over what could come next.

But the former Aberdeen midfielder has admitted a move to Ibrox is something he believes will eventually happen.

Asked about the prospect of following in the footsteps of his father and uncle, both former Rangers players, Ferguson said: “Ah, I know... Rangers? Let’s just say that sooner or later, I’ll go there; one day I know it’ll happen. [Gazzetta]

"The rest is about today: we’ve bounced back now, and we have to ride this wave.”

For now, though, Ferguson remains firmly committed to Bologna. The Scotland international revealed he received interest over the summer but ultimately decided to remain in Italy after reflecting on everything the club had given him.

45-cap Rangers star left out for Scotland clash as national boss reveals reason

Rangers learn match officials for Saturday night Premiership clash vs St Mirren

Rangers hero 'set' for new role at EFL side after leaving last club over summer

He explained: “I’d taken a bit of time out. I’d had some enquiries, yes, but I wanted to figure out exactly what to do with my life, whether to change direction or carry on as I was.

“Then I thought: Bologna has given me so much. On top of that, the Champions League, the Coppa Italia won and lifted as captain, the Europa League which... if we hadn’t come up against Aston Villa, we’d have reached the final, then the moments of friendship, even the tough times like the injury.

“In short: I took my time and then said just four words: Bologna is my home. And I want to stay here for at least another year.”

Ferguson later reiterated his affection for the Italian club while refusing to put a definitive timescale on his stay. He added: “I’m certainly not thinking about how long I’ll stay, but I’m definitely thinking about how I’ll stay.

"Bologna has been home since day one, I’ll say it again, and I’m having a brilliant time here.”

The midfielder has also embraced the responsibility of captaining Bologna, an achievement he described as a major source of pride as a Scotsman playing abroad.

#2121. “It’s not a surprise to me” – Pulisic delighted with Milan’s performance in derby win

Christian Pulisic believes AC Milan recorded an important win against Inter in the derby, but they must keep their heads down and continue working.

Milan claimed the bragging rights in the derby, winning 3-1 at San Siro tonight thanks to three goals in the first half. The first came from a Christian Pulisic header, the second was an Adrien Rabiot goal from a corner and the third was a Diego Moreira free-kick.

Alessandro Bastoni’s goal had briefly halved the deficit, but it was to be all for nothing as Milan racked up their fourth Derby della Madonnina win in a row. It moves the Rossoneri four points behind their city rivals, and also ends their unbeaten start to the season.

Pulisic spoke to DAZN after the full-time whistle to give his assessments on the game, and his words were relayed by MilanNews.

“We started the match very well, with intensity, with physicality. We played very well, scoring two goals in the first part, and this victory is very important for us.”

Four games, four goals, and four wins with Inter…

“I have to keep scoring in the derby, yes (laughs, ed.)”

“These are three very important points for us, but we have to continue to find this consistency and win every match.”

“Yes, we always play well in big games like today, so it’s not a surprise to me. We did things well.”

#2119. Why this season feels so uncertain as a Newcastle United fan

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Hope you are all doing well, I am in my 40s and a long time Newcastle United fan living in Australia.

I eventually got the chance in September to come and see my first game at St James’ Park against Hull – it was brilliant.

I watch all the matches, read, listen to pods etc and have played all my life (I’m 42).

I’m also into the tactical side of things and have undertaken some of my coaching badges here in Australia.

I’m sharing my first submission to The Mag about why I think this season feels so uncertain as a Newcastle United fan.

Newcastle United are a club of ups and downs – we all know that. The club’s current reality feels like we’re on the way down, though in reality it is more like a straight line from last season than any sort of significant change :

2026/27 13th place in the Premier League after 9 games. 11 points in those 9 games at an average of 1.22 points per game. 2025/26 12th place in the Premier League after 38 games. 49 points in those 38 games at an average of 1.28 points per game.

There are lots of reasons that this season feels more ominous than last season, though primarily it’s because we have no clear idea what to expect from this manager and from this group and players. We don’t know what to expect.

For Newcastle United fans, this season is full of unknowns.

Was Eddie Howe keeping our heads above water?

Who on earth are half of these new players?

Could we… go down, or could we actually end up being alright with a few tweaks?

Never in recent years have Newcastle United fans had so much to be uncertain about.

Under the management of Eddie Howe, there was certainty. We knew him and he knew us. There was no chance we were getting relegated under Howe, even through last season’s struggles.

We knew he knew the league. We knew he knew how to win games in this league. We knew he knew the histories, we knew he knew just what a cold, wet night in Stoke meant. We knew he could (mostly) improve players on an individual basis and get the best out of them. We knew the players respected him, liked him and trusted him. We knew his tactics and his style, and we knew they worked (mostly).

We knew Howe’s team. We knew that when the chips were down, Bruno would take the lead. We knew he’d demand the ball, that he’d try with every last ounce of determination and skill to create something, to inspire his teammates and to inspire the fans. We knew big Joe had his back and would kick someone if he had to, or even if he didn’t. We knew we had a threat up front or out wide to hurt opponents. We knew we had guys who could score goals in the Premier League. We knew Tripps wouldn’t stand for a team that didn’t give their all. We knew we had high standards, kept by high quality players who had done it all and seen it all.

Now, all that safety and certainty is gone and you know what – it’s freaking us out. Without the guard-rails that the certainty of Howe provided for us, we’re contemplating the worst. We’re scared of free fall. We’re not cautiously optimistic – we’re venturing towards riotously pessimistic.

So, now, after a similar start to last season in terms of points, we’re worried. Not worried like we were last year – this time it’s different. We’re worried because we’ve got no idea what comes next. We’ve got no idea how Matthias Jaissle responds or what he might do to get a tune out of this team. We’ve got no real indication yet that this group of players can actually deliver at this level, under any manager.

We don’t know how PIF, David Hopkinson and Ross Wilson will respond to this, because they haven’t had to before. We don’t fully know whether they even know what they’re doing to be honest. They seem to for the most part, but here we are nine league games in, with fingernails dwindling, a hard run of games ahead and a bunch of youngsters or also rans to take us through to the derby and Christmas and the crazy winter schedule..,so maybe they don’t know what they’re doing?

So, while we gaze into the unknown, let’s also think about the knowns. We know we’ve got a great set of fans. We know that when St James’ Park is rocking we can get the team over the line against almost anyone. We know this year they might well need that and they’ll need us behind them to succeed in this league.

We know we’re in transition. We know we care. We know we want the team to succeed whoever the manager is, wherever he’s from and whoever is on the pitch. We know it’s going to be turbulent because when has it ever not been? And we also know, we don’t want to support anyone else.

#2118. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Substitutes: Curd, Diakite, Kavuma-McQueen, Sarr, Walsh.Booked: Estêvão, Delap, Jackson, Geovany Quenda, Watson.Goals: Delap (42 pen, 62 pen), Antonio Glauder (89 og).

There will NOT be a penalty shootout. No one is quite sure why.

Anyway, that was an entertaining draw, plenty of good things for Chelsea (the play of Delap and Jackson) as well as worrying signs (open and vulnerable at the back).

The commentators on CFC TV are now not so sure!

That was an entertaining pre-season friendly. There was a bit of niggle and that added to the action.

There will be penalties, apparently, if it stays the same score...

Will there be a late winner? There will be four minutes of added time.

Mudryk just on picks up the ball on the left and, with four Chelsea players in the box, crosses into the danger area. It’s a good ball and asks too many questions of the hosts as Glauder diverts the ball into his own net.

It’s what the host have, on the balance of play, deserved, but it’s a gift from Chelsea. Essugo loses the ball in the final third and Bergson, on as sub pick it put driving at the box before hitting a low shot from outside the area, the ball nestling in the left corner of the net.

Chelsea have been better this half than the first 45, they’ve been able to control the pace of the game well since the break.

The pace has slowed down since the break, Chelsea seeing more of the ball. They work it right before Watson loses possession on the edge of the area.

The referee clearly forgot about the hydration break and the two teams are having a belated one now. Delightful...

I reckon there’s another goal left in this match. It’s been entertaining fare and the hosts have given as good as they’ve got, if not more.

This has been a lively match, better than most run-of-the-mill pre-season friendlies. Chelsea seeing a fair bit of possession at the moment, can they fashion a chance?

Yes they can. But it’s a longish shot from Gittens that is easily saved by Hamzi in the JDT goal.

More niggle in this match that hasn’t really had many tough challenges. After a few handbags the referee takes control and the argy bargy peters out.

It’s the least the hosts deserve. They have a free-kick 25 yards out, Arribas takes it with his right it’s at the wall but in turning away from the ball Delap deflects it into the far-right corner giving Slonina no chance.

Fluky goal but the hosts have deserved their bit of luck.

Delap again with the goal, this time he goes low, but still to the keeper’s right.

Penalty for Chelsea. Gittens cuts back in the box onto his right and is clipped by the defender. Clear-cut penalty.

Half-chance for Delap on the edge of the area. He playes a one-two with Jackson before opening up his body and letting fly, the shot going well wide.

Another good chance for the hosts and it’s not shock to write that it’s come from the industry of Arribas on the right. He fires in a low cross that evades everyone in the box.

Estevao goes down in the box, it looks as though it could well be a penalty but the referee waves play on. The Brazilian is the shown a yellow card for possibly lashing out having not got the decision he wanted.

The hosts have asserted themselves well this half, in much the same way as they did in the first 45 minutes.

Another good chance for the hosts and again it’s all too easy as Zahedi is one-on-one with the keeper. The striker, however, dithers a bit too long and Slonina makes a fine save. JDT have had plenty of chances to add to their sole goal...

Chelsea have had a ragged start to this half.

Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

#2117. Gallery: ‘Milan in ecstasy’, ‘A masterclass from Amorim’ – Today’s front pages in Italy

AC Milan pulled off a Halloween spectacular at San Siro last night as they beat city rivals Inter 3-1 in the derby.

All four goals came in the first half, with Christian Pulisic’s header and Adrien Rabiot’s flick from a corner putting Milan in dreamland less than 10 minutes in. Alessandro Bastoni halved the deficit, before Diego Moreira’s outstanding free-kick restored the two-goal lead.

QS: “Milan roar: a derby masterclass. Pulisic, Rabiot, and Moreira score in a 3-1 win over Inter: redemption for Amorim.”

#2116. Total Premier League minutes played by the 8 Newcastle United signings tells a story

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

A lot of focus on the eight Newcastle United signings that were brought in across summer 2026.

There were actually nine in total but teenager Ousmane Diabate was instantly loaned back to the selling club in Turkey in order to get regular first team football.

So what about these eight Newcastle United signings that have gone straight into the first team squad?

I have had a look at the minutes played so far this 2026-27 season by the new players.

Specifically, the minutes that each of the eight have played in the Premier League.

I think it tells a very clear story now we are nine Premier League matches (810 minutes) into this 2026-27 season.

Total Premier League minutes (out of a possible total of 810) played by the eight Newcastle United signings with breakdown match by match (Ev Everton, CP Crystal Palace, AV Aston Villa, Cov Coventry, H Hull, Le Leeds, B Bournemouth, T Tottenham, Li Liverpool):

0 Ewen Jaouen (Zero minutes in any of the nine Premier League matches)

115 Bazoumana Toure (3Ev, 34AV, 30Cov, 16H, 33Le)

256 Sean Steur (26Ev, 5CP, 66H, 71 Le, 13B, 19T, 56Li)

304 Matias Fernandez-Pardo (56AV, 90Cov, 74H, 57Le, 27B)

501 Nico Gonzalez (64Ev, 90CP, 90AV, 90Cov, 19Le, 77B, 71T)

536 Amar Dedic (87Ev, 90CP, 31Cov, 58Le, 90B, 90T, 90Li)

810 Lukas Hornicek (90Ev, 90CP, 90AV, 90Cov, 90H, 90Le, 90B, 90T, 90Li)

What stands out for me, is that Matthias Jaissle has given far more Premier League minutes to the (relatively) older and more experienced Newcastle United signings.

Three of the eight Newcastle United signings were aged 24 when they arrived, the other five were 21 or under.

Lukas Hornicek has played every Premier League minute this season.

Nico Gonzalez has started all seven EPL matches he has been available for.

Amar Dedic has started all of the EPL matches he was in a position to start, as well as off the bench against Coventry.

The other five Newcastle United signings who were aged 21 and under when they arrived at St James’ Park, have played 702 minutes between them. That is less than Lukas Hornicek alone has played and would also be less than the Dedic and Gonzalez individual totals if they had been available all of the time.

On the other hand, Matias Fernandez-Pardo has played far more minutes than I think he would have otherwise done so far, simply because of so many injured players in the early part of the season.

I am sure that Matthias Jaissle sees the exciting potential of Sean Steur just as much as we do, probably even more so considering he watches him every day in training. However, my belief is that the Head coach is simply trying to protect the 18-year-old from too much expectancy and pressure too soon. The same with the other younger players.

I don’t think he is holding the likes of Toure and Bamba back from playing more minutes so far because of any negative irrational reason, more a case of giving these younger inexperienced players from weaker leagues a chance to integrate and build up their confidence rather than throwing them in at the deep end and a case of sink or swim?

The booing from many Newcastle United fans at the Everton match for example, it isn’t exactly something that will help younger players to build confidence if they are subjected to that.
